q: Most common direction of glenohumeral dislocation?
e: About 95–97% of shoulder dislocations are anterior.

q: Nerve most commonly injured in anterior shoulder dislocation?
e: It winds round the surgical neck of the humerus; test sensation over the "regimental badge" area and deltoid contraction.

q: A Hill-Sachs lesion is an impaction defect of the:
e: It is produced as the humeral head is driven against the anterior glenoid rim during anterior dislocation.

q: A Bankart lesion is an avulsion/detachment of the:
o: Rotator cuff from the greater tuberosity
e: The essential lesion of recurrent anterior instability.

q: The rotator cuff tendon most commonly torn is:
e: It runs beneath the acromion and is the usual site of impingement and degenerative tears.

q: The painful arc of subacromial impingement lies between:
e: Pain appears as the greater tuberosity passes under the coracoacromial arch.

q: Which test assesses subscapularis function?
e: Lift-off and belly-press tests test subscapularis; Jobe tests supraspinatus.

q: The commonest site of clavicle fracture is the:
e: About 80% of clavicle fractures are in the middle third, at the junction of two curvatures.

q: Erb's palsy results from injury to roots:
e: Waiter's-tip posture: adducted, internally rotated shoulder, extended elbow, pronated forearm.

q: Klumpke's paralysis involves roots:
e: Claw hand and Horner syndrome if T1 sympathetic fibres are involved.

q: Winging of the scapula is due to paralysis of which muscle/nerve?
e: Medial border winging appears when pushing against a wall (serratus anterior); trapezius palsy gives lateral winging.

q: Rockwood classification is used for injuries of the:
e: Types I–VI, from sprain to subcoracoid/subacromial displacement.

q: Which movement is most restricted in adhesive capsulitis (frozen shoulder)?
e: Global capsular restriction with external rotation lost first and most.

q: Sprengel deformity is:
e: Often associated with an omovertebral bar and Klippel–Feil syndrome.

q: Neer's classification of proximal humeral fractures counts a part displaced by more than:
e: Four parts: articular segment, greater tuberosity, lesser tuberosity, shaft.

q: Commonest direction of elbow dislocation?
e: Usually from a fall on the outstretched hand; coronoid and radial head fractures may accompany it.

q: Nerve most commonly injured in extension-type supracondylar fracture of the humerus in children:
e: Anterior interosseous palsy gives loss of pinch ("OK" sign); radial nerve is commonly injured in some series too.

q: Gunstock deformity is a result of malunion of:
a: Supracondylar fracture of the humerus (cubitus varus)
e: Varus and internal-rotation malunion; lateral-condyle non-union gives cubitus valgus and late ulnar palsy.

q: Volkmann's ischaemic contracture involves chiefly which muscles?
a: Deep flexors (FDP, FPL) of the forearm
e: Ischaemia of the flexor compartment after supracondylar fracture or tight cast.

q: Monteggia fracture-dislocation is:
a: Proximal ulna fracture with radial head dislocation
o: Radius shaft fracture with distal radioulnar dislocation
Radial head fracture with interosseous rupture
e: Bado classification; the radial head must be reduced by ulna fixation.

q: Galeazzi fracture is:
a: Radius shaft fracture with distal radioulnar joint dislocation
o: Ulna shaft fracture with radial head dislocation
Distal radius fracture with carpal subluxation
Olecranon fracture with ulnar nerve palsy
e: Called the "fracture of necessity" because it needs operation in adults.

q: 'Pulled elbow' (nursemaid's elbow) is a subluxation of the:
a: Radial head through the annular ligament
e: Typically at 1–4 years after a sudden longitudinal pull; treat by supination–flexion reduction.

q: Tennis elbow (lateral epicondylitis) involves degeneration at the origin of:
e: Pain on resisted wrist extension; Cozen's and Mill's tests are positive.

q: Golfer's elbow affects the common origin of the:
a: Flexor–pronator group at the medial epicondyle
o: Extensor group at the lateral epicondyle
e: Medial epicondylitis; the ulnar nerve lies close behind the epicondyle.

q: The first ossification centre to appear at the elbow is the:
e: CRITOE: Capitellum, Radial head, Internal epicondyle, Trochlea, Olecranon, External epicondyle.

q: Essex-Lopresti injury consists of:
a: Radial head fracture with interosseous membrane tear and DRUJ disruption
o: Olecranon fracture with ulnar nerve palsy
Supracondylar fracture with brachial artery injury
e: Never excise the radial head alone in this injury.

q: Cubital tunnel syndrome compresses the:
e: Tinel's sign at the medial epicondyle and weak grip/intrinsics are features.

q: Most commonly fractured carpal bone?
e: Tenderness in the anatomical snuffbox after a fall on the outstretched hand.

q: The major complication of scaphoid waist fracture is:
a: Avascular necrosis of the proximal pole
e: Blood supply enters distally (dorsal carpal branch of the radial artery) and runs retrograde.

q: The classic deformity of Colles fracture is the:
e: Extra-articular distal radius fracture with dorsal displacement and dorsal tilt.

q: Smith's fracture is:
a: Distal radius fracture with volar displacement
o: Distal radius fracture with dorsal displacement
Fracture of base of first metacarpal
e: Reverse Colles; garden-spade deformity; often needs volar plating.

q: Barton's fracture is:
a: Intra-articular marginal fracture of the distal radius with carpal subluxation
o: Fracture of the first metacarpal base
Fracture of the hook of hamate
e: Dorsal or volar rim fracture; unstable and needs fixation.

q: Kienböck's disease is avascular necrosis of the:
e: Associated with negative ulnar variance; Lichtman classification.

q: Preiser's disease is avascular necrosis of the:
e: Idiopathic AVN of the scaphoid without fracture.

q: De Quervain's tenosynovitis involves the tendons of:
a: Abductor pollicis longus and extensor pollicis brevis
o: Extensor pollicis longus and extensor indicis
Flexor pollicis longus and flexor carpi radialis
Extensor carpi radialis longus and brevis
e: First dorsal compartment; Finkelstein's test is positive.

q: Dupuytren's contracture is a disease of the:
e: Ring finger is most commonly involved, then the little finger.

q: Carpal tunnel syndrome is compression of the:
a: Median nerve beneath the flexor retinaculum
o: Radial nerve at the spiral groove
Anterior interosseous nerve at the elbow
e: Night tingling in the radial three and a half digits; Phalen's and Tinel's signs; thenar wasting late.

q: Bennett's fracture is:
a: Intra-articular fracture-dislocation of the base of the first metacarpal
o: Fracture of the neck of the fifth metacarpal
Fracture of the hook of hamate
Avulsion of the volar plate of the PIP joint
e: The volar-ulnar fragment stays in place; abductor pollicis longus pulls the shaft proximally and radially.

q: A 'boxer's fracture' is a fracture of the:
o: Shaft of the proximal phalanx of the thumb
e: Accept up to about 40° of angulation in the fifth metacarpal neck.

q: Mallet finger results from rupture/avulsion of the:
a: Extensor tendon at its insertion on the distal phalanx
o: FDP tendon at the distal phalanx
Central slip at the PIP joint
Collateral ligament of the DIP joint
e: Treated with continuous extension splinting of the DIP joint for about 6–8 weeks.

q: 'Jersey finger' is avulsion of:
o: Ulnar collateral ligament of the thumb
e: Seen in rugby/football tackling; FDP retracts into palm.

q: Trigger finger occurs at which pulley?
e: Nodule on flexor tendon catching at the A1 pulley; treat with steroid injection or release.

q: Froment's sign tests which muscle/nerve?
o: Flexor pollicis longus — anterior interosseous nerve
e: Flexion of the thumb IP joint (FPL, median nerve) substitutes for weak adductor pollicis when gripping paper.

q: 'Hand of benediction' occurs on attempting to make a fist after injury to the:
e: Index and middle fingers cannot flex because FDP/FDS to those fingers are paralysed.

q: 'Wrist drop' is caused by injury to the:
e: Typically at the spiral groove in mid-shaft humeral fracture (Holstein–Lewis fracture at the distal third).

q: 'Skier's thumb' (gamekeeper's thumb) is injury of the:
a: Ulnar collateral ligament of the thumb MCP joint
o: Radial collateral ligament of the thumb CMC joint
Volar plate of the PIP joint
e: Stener lesion: adductor aponeurosis interposed between torn ligament and bone.

q: Scapholunate dissociation produces which radiographic sign?
e: Along with the cortical ring sign and increased scapholunate angle (> 60°).

q: The normal radial inclination and volar tilt of the distal radius are about:
e: Radial height ≈ 11–12 mm; restoring these is the aim of fixation.

q: Commonest site of tuberculosis of the spine?
e: Paradiscal lesion with anterior wedging leads to kyphosis (gibbus); Pott paraplegia.

q: A Chance fracture is:
a: Flexion–distraction injury through the vertebral body (seat-belt injury)
o: Compression fracture of an osteoporotic vertebra
e: Associated with intra-abdominal injury; occurs at the thoracolumbar junction.

q: Jefferson's fracture is a:
a: Burst fracture of the ring of C1 (atlas)
e: Axial loading; widening of the lateral masses (> 7 mm combined) suggests transverse ligament rupture.

q: A 'hangman's fracture' involves the:
e: Hyperextension–distraction; traumatic spondylolisthesis of C2.

q: Type II odontoid fracture lies through the:
o: Body of C2 below the dens
e: Highest risk of non-union because of the watershed blood supply.

q: Cauda equina syndrome presents with:
a: Saddle anaesthesia, bladder retention and bilateral leg weakness
o: Loss of position sense in one leg only
e: A surgical emergency — decompress within 24–48 h.

q: The commonest level of lumbar disc prolapse is:
e: Followed by L5–S1; the L4–5 disc usually compresses the traversing L5 root (posterolateral prolapse).

q: Straight-leg raising is positive in sciatica between about:
e: Pain before 30° or after 70° is unlikely to be root tension; bowstring and crossed SLR add specificity.

q: The commonest level and type of spondylolisthesis in children and adolescents is:
e: Severity graded by Meyerding (I–V).

q: The measurement used to quantify scoliosis is the:
e: Bracing is considered for curves of about 25–40° in growing children; surgery above about 45–50°.

q: Scheuermann's disease is:
a: Juvenile thoracic kyphosis with wedging of ≥ 5° in three adjacent vertebrae
e: Rigid kyphosis in adolescence; bracing is for growing patients.

q: Brown-Séquard syndrome causes:
a: Ipsilateral motor and proprioception loss, contralateral pain and temperature loss
o: Bilateral flaccid paralysis with sensory sparing
Loss of pain and temperature in a cape distribution only
e: Hemisection of the cord; best prognosis of incomplete cord syndromes.

q: Central cord syndrome typically shows:
a: Greater weakness in the upper limbs than the lower limbs
o: Greater weakness in the lower limbs
Complete motor loss with intact pain sensation
e: Hyperextension injury in an older patient with cervical spondylosis.

q: On the ASIA impairment scale, grade A means:
a: Complete — no motor or sensory function in S4–S5
o: Incomplete — motor useful in most muscles
e: Sacral sparing defines an incomplete injury.

q: Denis's 'three-column' concept: the middle column consists of:
a: Posterior vertebral body wall, posterior annulus and PLL
o: Anterior longitudinal ligament and anterior half of the body
e: Failure of the middle column defines instability.

q: The commonest hip dislocation is:
e: Dashboard injury: hip flexed, adducted and internally rotated.

q: Deformity in posterior dislocation of the hip:
a: Flexion, adduction, internal rotation and shortening
e: Reduce within 6 hours to lower the risk of AVN.

q: Nerve at risk in posterior hip dislocation:
e: Foot drop is the usual presentation.

q: The classic complication of displaced femoral neck fracture is:
a: Avascular necrosis of the femoral head
e: Retinacular vessels (medial femoral circumflex artery) are disrupted.

q: Garden classification is used for:
e: Garden I–II undisplaced, III–IV displaced.

q: Perthes disease is avascular necrosis of the femoral head, typically at age:
e: Catterall and Herring (lateral pillar) classifications; children < 6 years do well.

q: Slipped capital femoral epiphysis most commonly occurs in:
e: Klein's line fails to intersect the epiphysis; treat by in-situ pinning.

q: Ortolani's test is positive when:
a: A dislocated hip is reduced with a clunk
o: A reduced hip is dislocated by posterior pressure
The thigh shows asymmetric skin folds
e: Barlow's is the provocative test that dislocates an unstable hip.

q: A positive Trendelenburg sign indicates weakness of:
e: The pelvis drops on the side of the lifted leg.

q: Preferred treatment of stable intertrochanteric fracture in adults:
a: Dynamic hip screw or cephalomedullary nail
e: Early fixation allows early mobilisation; unstable patterns favour intramedullary nails.

q: Thomas's test demonstrates:
a: Fixed flexion deformity of the hip
e: Flex the opposite hip to flatten the lumbar lordosis; the tested thigh rises.

q: Acetabular fractures are classified by:
e: Elementary and associated patterns related to the anterior and posterior columns.

q: Pelvic ring injuries are classified by:
e: Lateral compression, AP compression and vertical shear mechanisms.

q: The 'unhappy triad' of O'Donoghue consists of:
e: Valgus–external rotation injury (some authors now note the lateral meniscus is more often torn).

q: Lachman's test examines the:
e: Performed at 20–30° of flexion; the most sensitive clinical test for ACL.

q: A positive posterior drawer test indicates:
e: Posterior sag sign is also seen.

q: McMurray's test is used to detect:
e: A palpable click or pain on rotation while extending the flexed knee.

q: A Segond fracture is an avulsion of the:
a: Lateral tibial plateau (strongly associated with ACL rupture)
e: Pathognomonic radiographic sign of ACL injury.

q: Pellegrini–Stieda lesion is calcification of the:
a: Medial collateral ligament near the femoral attachment
e: Seen after old MCL injury.

q: Osgood–Schlatter disease is traction apophysitis of the:
e: Adolescent athletes; rest and quadriceps stretching.

q: Sinding-Larsen-Johansson disease affects the:
e: Traction apophysitis of the patellar tendon origin.

q: Tibial plateau fractures are classified by:
e: Types I–VI; type II (split-depression of the lateral plateau) is commonest.

q: Blount's disease is:
e: Abnormal growth of the posteromedial proximal tibial physis.

q: Patellar dislocation is usually in which direction?
e: Positive patellar apprehension test; MPFL tear on MRI.

q: A Baker's cyst lies between:
a: Semimembranosus and the medial head of gastrocnemius
o: Biceps femoris and the lateral head of gastrocnemius
e: Communicates with the knee joint; ruptured cyst mimics deep vein thrombosis.

q: Femoral shaft fractures in adults are best treated by:
e: Fat embolism and blood loss are the key early complications.

q: The normal Böhler angle of the calcaneum is:
e: It is reduced or flattened in comminuted calcaneal fractures.

q: 'Lover's fracture' refers to the association of calcaneal fracture with:
e: Both result from axial loading in a fall from height.

q: Hawkins classification applies to:
e: Higher grades predict avascular necrosis of the talar body (Hawkins sign on X-ray).

q: Lisfranc injury is an injury of the:
e: Fleck sign: avulsion at the base of the second metatarsal.

q: A Jones fracture is a fracture of the:
a: Metaphyseal–diaphyseal junction of the fifth metatarsal
o: Shaft of the second metatarsal (march fracture)
e: Poor blood supply; high rate of non-union, often treated by intramedullary screw.

q: Danis–Weber classification of ankle fractures is based on the level of the fibular fracture relative to the:
e: Type A below, B at, and C above the syndesmosis.

q: The test for Achilles tendon rupture is the:
e: Absent plantar flexion on squeezing the calf.

q: The components of the clubfoot (CTEV) deformity are:
e: Ponseti casting corrects them in sequence: cavus first, equinus last (with tenotomy).

q: Morton's neuroma classically occurs in which web space?
e: Perineural fibrosis of the common digital nerve; Mulder click.

q: Foot drop is typically caused by injury to the:
a: Common peroneal nerve at the neck of the fibula
o: Tibial nerve at the tarsal tunnel
e: Loss of ankle dorsiflexion and eversion with high-stepping gait.

q: Sever's disease is:
o: Osteochondritis of the second metatarsal head
e: Heel pain in active 8–12-year-olds, settles with rest and heel cups.

q: Freiberg's disease affects the:
e: Osteochondrosis presenting with forefoot pain in adolescents, mainly girls.

q: Köhler's disease is osteochondritis of the:
e: Occurs in boys of about 4–6 years; self-limiting.

q: How many fascial compartments does the leg have?
a: Four (anterior, lateral, superficial and deep posterior)
e: Compartment syndrome needs fasciotomy of all four compartments.

q: The commonest site of primary osteosarcoma is:
a: Around the knee (distal femur / proximal tibia)
e: Metaphyseal; sunburst periosteal reaction and Codman triangle.

q: Ewing's sarcoma shows which periosteal reaction and translocation?
e: Diaphyseal permeative lesion in children with fever and raised ESR.

q: A giant cell tumour typically occurs in the:
a: Epiphysis of a long bone after skeletal maturity
e: 'Soap-bubble' appearance; commonest around the knee and distal radius.

q: Osteoid osteoma pain is typically:
a: Worse at night and relieved by aspirin/NSAIDs
e: A small nidus (< 1.5 cm) with surrounding sclerosis; treated by radiofrequency ablation or excision.

q: Commonest organism of acute haematogenous osteomyelitis in children:
e: Salmonella is classically associated with sickle-cell disease.

q: Rickets results from deficiency of:
e: Widened, cupped physes, rachitic rosary and bow legs.

q: The commonest Salter–Harris fracture type is:
e: Fracture through the physis with a metaphyseal fragment (Thurston–Holland).

q: Gustilo–Anderson type IIIC open fracture means:
a: Open fracture with arterial injury needing repair
o: Wound 1–10 cm without extensive soft-tissue damage
e: Highest rate of amputation and infection.

q: The classic triad of fat embolism syndrome is:
a: Respiratory distress, neurological changes and petechial rash
e: Usually appears 24–72 h after long-bone fracture.

q: Compartment syndrome is chiefly diagnosed by:
a: Pain out of proportion, aggravated by passive stretch
e: Pulses are usually present; delta pressure < 30 mmHg supports the diagnosis.

q: Seddon's classification of nerve injury includes:
e: Wallerian degeneration occurs in axonotmesis and neurotmesis; neurapraxia recovers fully.

q: The stages of fracture healing in sequence are:
a: Haematoma, inflammation, soft callus, hard callus, remodelling
o: Inflammation, remodelling, hard callus, soft callus
Haematoma, hard callus, soft callus, remodelling
e: Primary (direct) healing occurs only with absolute stability and no gap.
